hist_aqa.3.0.summary: The 1920s in America was a decade of unprecedented economic growth known as the 'Boom', fueled by mass production techniques, aggressive advertising, and the convenient new system of hire purchase. Republican economic policies of laissez-faire, high tariffs, and low taxes created a pro-business climate that culminated in a massive stock market boom. However, this prosperity was deeply unequal, bypassing farmers, traditional industries, and African-Americans, setting the stage for future economic vulnerability.

core.p: Mass production revolutionised American manufacturing during the 1920s, enabling factories to produce goods on an unprecedented scale and at greatly reduced costs. Pioneered by Henry Ford in the automotive industry, these techniques transformed the US economy and made luxury items accessible to ordinary working people.
bullets: Henry Ford introduced the moving assembly line at his Highland Park plant in Michigan in 1913, which was widely adopted across industries in the 1920s.
The assembly line broke complex manufacturing tasks down into simple, repetitive steps, drastically reducing the time needed to build a product.
The time required to build a Ford Model T dropped from 12 hours to just 93 minutes by 1914, and prices fell from $850 in 1908 to under $300 by the 1920s.
By 1929, over 20 million cars were on American roads, creating a massive multiplier effect that stimulated related industries like steel, rubber, glass, and road building.

callouts.p: The manufacture of goods in large quantities using machinery and assembly lines.
Nicknamed the 'Tin Lizzie', it became the symbol of American mass production. By 1920, half of all cars in the world were Ford Model Ts.

core.p: The boom in manufacturing created a flood of new consumer goods that Americans were eager to buy. To sustain this high level of purchasing, modern advertising agencies emerged on Madison Avenue, using psychological techniques to convince consumers that owning these new products was essential for modern living.
bullets: New household appliances like vacuum cleaners, washing machines, refrigerators, and radios transformed domestic life and created huge demand.
Advertising shifted from merely informing buyers about products to manipulating their desires, exploiting insecurities about hygiene, social status, and aging.
Radio, billboards, and glossy magazines like the Saturday Evening Post saturated American daily life with powerful commercial messages.
Consumerism became the defining feature of the American identity, where social worth was increasingly measured by what people owned rather than who they were.

callouts.p: A social and economic order that encourages the acquisition of goods and services in ever-greater amounts.
Always connect consumerism to mass production and hire purchase in an essay to show how supply and demand were artificially linked.

core.p: Although wages rose for many industrial workers, the cost of expensive new consumer durables like cars and radios still far outstripped immediate savings. To solve this problem and keep factories producing at maximum capacity, the system of hire purchase and easy credit was massively expanded.
bullets: Hire purchase allowed buyers to pay a small deposit and pay off the remaining balance in regular, manageable instalments plus interest.
By the end of the 1920s, an estimated 75% of all cars and a high percentage of furniture and appliances were bought on credit.
While hire purchase fueled the short-term economic boom by bringing future earnings into present spending, it created a dangerous culture of personal debt.
When the economy faltered, consumers who had maxed out their credit could no longer buy new goods, causing manufacturing orders to collapse.

callouts.p: A system where a buyer pays for a manufactured good in instalments while enjoying the use of it during the payment period.
Do not confuse hire purchase with buying on the margin. Hire purchase is for consumer goods; buying on the margin is for stocks.

core.p: Throughout the 1920s, the US government was led by three pro-business Republican presidents: Warren Harding (1921–1923), Calvin Coolidge (1923–1929), and Herbert Hoover (1929–1933). Their governing philosophy was firmly rooted in laissez-faire capitalism and active support for American industry.
bullets: Presidents believed in 'rugged individualism', the idea that people should succeed through their own efforts without government handouts or interference.
The Fordney-McCumber Tariff of 1922 placed record-high protective duties on foreign imports, forcing Americans to buy domestically produced goods.
Secretaries of the Treasury like Andrew Mellon cut taxes for the wealthy and corporations, arguing that 'trickle-down' wealth would be reinvested in factories and create jobs.
The government systematically weakened trade unions through anti-union court rulings and 'yellow-dog contracts', keeping labour costs low and profits high.

callouts.p: The economic policy of leaving things to take their own course, without government intervention or regulation.
Harding, Coolidge, and Hoover summarized their approach with the famous slogan: 'The business of America is business.'

core.p: The dizzying profits of corporations fueled an unprecedented frenzy of speculation on the Wall Street stock market. Ordinary Americans and wealthy investors alike began treating the stock market like a casino, driving share prices far beyond the actual, underlying value of the companies.
bullets: Between 1925 and 1929, the value of stocks on the New York Stock Exchange more than doubled, creating an illusion of permanent, effortless wealth.
Speculation was supercharged by 'buying on the margin', where investors could buy shares by paying as little as 10% in cash and borrowing the remaining 90% from brokers.
People from all walks of life—clerks, chauffeurs, and teachers—poured their life savings into stocks or quit their jobs to play the market full-time.
As long as stock prices kept rising, brokers could reclaim their loans when the shares were sold, but this house of cards depended entirely on endless price growth.

callouts.p: Purchasing stocks with borrowed money (often up to 90% of the cost) with the expectation that the shares would rise quickly to pay off the loan.
Explain how buying on the margin linked Wall Street speculation directly to the eventual Wall Street Crash when prices stopped rising.

core.p: Despite the glittering surface of the 1920s Boom, prosperity was dangerously lopsided. While a tiny minority accumulated astronomical fortunes, millions of working Americans and traditional sectors of the economy were left far behind, creating a fragile foundation for the national economy.
bullets: By 1929, the richest 1% of Americans owned roughly 33% of the nation's wealth, while over 42% of families lived below the poverty line of $2,000 a year.
Traditional industries like coal mining, textiles, and shipbuilding suffered due to overproduction and competition from new synthetics and electricity.
Agriculture experienced a severe depression throughout the 1920s due to overproduction after WWI, falling European demand, and mechanisation.
African-Americans, migrant workers, and recent immigrants were trapped in low-wage jobs, unable to participate in the consumer revolution or share market.

callouts.p: Producing more goods or crops than consumers are able or willing to buy, leading to crashing prices.
Students often write 'everyone got rich in the 1920s'. Make sure to emphasise that the Boom was deeply unequal and bypassed millions.

analogy.t: The 1920s American Economy as a High-Speed Rollercoaster
analogy.p: Imagine a rollercoaster engineered by enthusiastic mechanics (Republican policies) who remove the brakes and weld the throttle wide open (mass production and hire purchase). The cart rockets up the track (stock market boom) propelled by adrenaline and borrowed money. However, the front cars (wealthy industrialists and speculators) enjoy all the luxury, while the back cars (farmers, textile workers, miners) rattle violently on decaying tracks. Where the analogy breaks down is that a rollercoaster eventually stops safely at a station, whereas the 1920s economic ride ended in a catastrophic derailment (the Wall Street Crash of 1929).

terms.d: The manufacture of goods in large quantities using machinery and assembly lines.
A manufacturing process where parts are added sequentially as the semi-finished assembly moves down a line.
A system of paying for goods by instalments while enjoying use of them immediately.
A social and economic order that encourages the acquisition of goods in ever-greater amounts.
The economic doctrine that government should not interfere in the marketplace.
A tax or duty placed on imported foreign goods to protect domestic industries.
Buying high-risk stocks or assets with borrowed money in the hope of making a quick, massive profit.
Purchasing stocks with a small cash deposit (e.g., 10%) and borrowing the rest from brokers.
The accumulation of unsaleable goods because manufacturing output outstrips consumer purchasing power.
The belief that individuals can succeed unaided and that government help destroys self-reliance.

mistakes.w: Saying that the Wall Street Crash caused the 1920s Boom.
mistakes.r: The Boom happened first (1920–1929) and was caused by mass production and consumerism; the stock market boom was a symptom that crashed at the very end of the decade.

mistakes.w: Confusing hire purchase with buying on the margin.
mistakes.r: Hire purchase is for buying physical consumer goods (cars, radios) on credit; buying on the margin is for buying shares on the stock market using borrowed money.

mistakes.w: Writing that all Americans experienced great wealth during the 1920s.
mistakes.r: The wealth was heavily concentrated; over 40% of Americans lived in poverty, and farmers and traditional industries suffered a depression.

mistakes.w: Stating that the Democratic presidents caused the 1920s economic policies.
mistakes.r: The 1920s were governed exclusively by pro-business Republican presidents: Harding, Coolidge, and Hoover.

mistakes.w: Thinking Henry Ford invented the car.
mistakes.r: Ford did not invent the car; he revolutionised its manufacture by introducing the moving assembly line, making it affordable for the masses.

exam.q: Describe two features of mass production in the 1920s.
model: Feature: One mark for identifying a feature (e.g., the moving assembly line).
Detail: One mark for supporting historical detail (e.g., introduced by Henry Ford, breaking production down into simple, repetitive tasks).
Second feature: One mark for identifying a second feature (e.g., standardisation of parts).
Second detail: One mark for supporting historical detail (e.g., drastically reduced production time and lowered the cost of goods like the Model T).
exam.tip: Keep descriptions concise. Two distinct features with valid historical detail will secure full marks.

exam.q: In what ways were the lives of Americans affected by the economic boom of the 1920s? Explain your answer.
model: Analytical point 1: Many Americans experienced a massive rise in living standards due to new consumer goods like radios, vacuum cleaners, and automobiles.
Supporting evidence 1: Mass production and hire purchase made luxury items accessible; over 20 million cars were on the road by 1929.
Analytical point 2: However, not all Americans shared in this prosperity, as deep wealth inequality persisted.
Supporting evidence 2: Farmers suffered from agricultural depression and overproduction, and over 40% of families lived below the poverty line.
Conclusion linking back to the question: While the urban middle class enjoyed unprecedented material comfort, traditional workers and farmers were left behind.
exam.tip: To hit top band (Level 4), you must provide balanced analysis covering both the positive impacts of the boom and the limits or inequalities.

exam.q: Which of the following was the more important reason for the economic boom of the 1920s: mass production or Republican economic policies?
model: Factor 1 analysis (Mass production): Explain how assembly lines lowered manufacturing costs, created a multiplier effect, and flooded the market with affordable goods.
Factor 2 analysis (Republican policies): Explain how laissez-faire, high protective tariffs (Fordney-McCumber), and tax cuts created a pro-business environment.

Comparative judgment: Argue that mass production was the fundamental engine of the boom because it created the actual goods people wanted, but acknowledge that Republican policies provided the vital framework that allowed businesses to thrive without government interference.
exam.tip: For a 12-mark 'Write an account' or 'Which was more important' style question, evaluate both options explicitly and reach a justified, sustained conclusion.

exam.q: Explain why the stock market boom occurred in the late 1920s.
model: Reason 1: Corporate profits soared due to mass production and consumer spending, leading investors to believe stock values would rise forever.
Reason 2: The practice of 'buying on the margin' allowed ordinary people to speculate with borrowed money, pumping artificial money into the stock exchange.
exam.tip: Focus strictly on why the boom happened, mentioning speculation and margin buying without drifting into the 1929 crash.

hist_aqa.3.8.summary: This topic covers the transformative social policies of the 1960s and 1970s, focusing on John F. Kennedy's New Frontier, Lyndon B. Johnson's Great Society, and the major milestones of the second-wave feminist movement. Students must understand how federal legislation attempted to tackle poverty and discrimination, alongside the legal battles for women's liberation, reproductive rights, and constitutional equality.

core.p: Elected in 1960, John F. Kennedy introduced the 'New Frontier' domestic policy, aiming to tackle poverty, unemployment, and civil rights through federal intervention and economic stimulation.
bullets: Focused on revitalising the economy through deficit spending, tax cuts, and funding for public works.
Created the Peace Corps in 1961 to send young American volunteers to developing nations to assist with education, health, and agriculture.
Increased funding for space exploration, culminating in the goal to land a man on the moon.
Faced significant opposition in Congress from a coalition of Southern Democrats and Republicans who blocked healthcare reform and federal aid to education.
Established the President's Commission on the Status of Women in 1961, which highlighted widespread discrimination in employment and education.

callouts.p: JFK struggled to pass much of his New Frontier legislation because conservative Southern Democrats and Republicans viewed federal spending and social reform as too expensive and government-heavy.
JFK's domestic policy programme designed to improve the economy, education, healthcare, and civil rights.

core.p: Following JFK's assassination in 1963, President Lyndon B. Johnson used his formidable political skill to push through the most ambitious legislative agenda since the New Deal, known as the 'Great Society'.
bullets: Aimed to end poverty and racial injustice in the United States, declaring an 'unconditional war on poverty'.
Economic Opportunity Act (1964) created the Office of Economic Opportunity (OEO) to fund job training and community action programmes like Job Corps and Head Start.
Medicare (1965) provided federally funded health insurance for Americans aged 65 and older.
Medicaid (1965) provided health insurance for low-income families and individuals.
Elementary and Secondary Education Act (1965) provided major federal funding for schools in impoverished districts.

head: Programme
Target Group / Purpose
Impact
rows: Guaranteed medical care, reduced elderly poverty from medical bills.
Provided vital healthcare access to millions living in poverty.
Provided early education to bridge the achievement gap before school.

callouts.p: LBJ's Great Society successfully reduced the percentage of Americans living below the poverty line significantly during the mid-to-late 1960s.
Do not confuse the New Deal (Roosevelt, 1930s, Depression) with the Great Society (Johnson, 1960s, affluence and civil rights).

core.h: Limitations and Criticisms of the Great Society
core.p: Despite its noble aims and significant achievements in reducing poverty and improving healthcare, the Great Society faced severe criticism and financial strain by the late 1960s.
bullets: The escalating cost of the Vietnam War severely drained federal funds away from Great Society social programmes.
Critics argued that welfare dependency was being encouraged and that the federal government was interfering too much in local and personal affairs.
Urban riots in Watts (Los Angeles) and Detroit showed that poverty and discrimination were not solved by legislation alone.
Conservative backlash began to grow, setting the stage for the rise of law-and-order politics under Richard Nixon in 1968.
Many radicals felt the reforms did not go far enough to dismantle systemic capitalist and racial inequalities.

core.p: The 1960s saw the emergence of second-wave feminism, which sought to challenge social, cultural, and economic inequalities beyond the right to vote won in 1920.
bullets: Betty Friedan published 'The Feminine Mystique' in 1963, which challenged the domestic ideal that women found fulfillment solely as wives and mothers ('the problem that has no name').
The Civil Rights Act of 1964 included Title VII, which prohibited employment discrimination on the basis of sex (though initially added as a joke by opponents to sink the bill).
Activists demanded equal pay for equal work, reproductive freedom, and an end to discrimination in higher education and professional careers.
Grassroots consciousness-raising groups helped women articulate shared grievances about domestic expectations and systemic sexism.

callouts.p: A period of feminist activity during the 1960s and 1970s that focused on workplace equality, family, sexuality, and reproductive rights.

core.p: Founded in 1966 by Betty Friedan, Pauli Murray, and other activists, the National Organization for Women became the primary lobbying group for the feminist movement.
bullets: Modelled after the NAACP, NOW used legal action, lobbying, and public demonstrations to enforce Title VII of the Civil Rights Act.
Campooned against sex-segregated 'Help Wanted' job advertisements in newspapers, winning a landmark 1969 ruling that banned the practice.
Fought for maternity leave rights, federally funded childcare centres, and access to contraception and abortion.
Disagreed internally at times; more radical feminists split off to protest beauty pageants and demand more revolutionary changes to patriarchal structures.
By the 1970s, NOW had tens of thousands of members and significant political influence.

callouts.p: NOW operated within the political system using lobbying and litigation, distinguishing it from more radical feminist groups who used direct action protests.

core.p: The Supreme Court case Roe v. Wade was a watershed legal victory for the feminist movement, establishing a constitutional right to abortion.
bullets: Norma McCorvey (using the legal pseudonym 'Jane Roe') sued Henry Wade, the district attorney of Dallas County, Texas, challenging state laws criminalising abortion.
The Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that the U.S. Constitution's 14th Amendment's Due Process Clause protects an individual's right to privacy, encompassing a woman's right to choose to have an abortion.
Established a trimester framework: states could not ban abortion in the first trimester, but could regulate it in the second and third to protect maternal health or fetal life.
Sparked intense and long-lasting backlash from religious conservatives and the anti-abortion ('pro-life') movement, which mobilized politically through the religious right.
Deeply polarized American politics for decades to come.

callouts.p: The 1973 Supreme Court ruling that legalized abortion nationwide based on the constitutional right to privacy.

core.h: The Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) and Anti-Feminist Backlash
core.p: The Equal Rights Amendment sought to constitutionally guarantee gender equality, but its failure highlighted the strength of the emerging conservative backlash.
bullets: First proposed in 1923 by Alice Paul, the ERA stated: 'Equality of rights under the law shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex.'
Passed Congress overwhelmingly in 1972 and was sent to the states for ratification, needing 38 state approvals.
Faced fierce opposition led by conservative activist Phyllis Schlafly and her 'STOP ERA' campaign.
Schlafly argued that the ERA would strip women of traditional protections like exemption from the military draft, alimony, and protective labor laws, while destroying the traditional family.
Despite extensions, the ERA fell short of the 38-state threshold by the 1982 deadline, marking a major defeat for the feminist movement.

callouts.p: Schlafly successfully organized grassroots conservative women to defeat the ERA by arguing it undermined traditional gender roles and family values.

analogy.t: The Great Society and Feminist Movement as Building a Modern House
analogy.p: JFK and LBJ's Great Society were like building a secure, well-equipped house for impoverished citizens by installing new plumbing (Medicare) and electricity (Federal aid to education). Meanwhile, second-wave feminism and groups like NOW were like tearing down interior walls that restricted certain residents to only working in the kitchen, demanding equal access to every room in the house. Where the analogy breaks down is that building a house follows a blueprint, whereas social reform and civil rights faced bitter, violent resistance and endless legal battles over who had the right to live there.

terms.d: JFK's domestic legislative programme aimed at economic growth, social welfare, and civil rights.
LBJ's sweeping domestic reform programme (1964–1968) aimed at ending poverty and racial injustice.
A federal health insurance programme established in 1965 for Americans aged 65 and older.
A federal and state assistance programme established in 1965 that pays for medical care for low-income people.
The feminist movement of the 1960s and 1970s focusing on workplace equality, sexuality, family, and reproductive rights.
Betty Friedan's 1963 book that challenged domesticity and sparked second-wave feminism.
National Organization for Women; founded in 1966 to campaign for women's equality and enforce Title VII.
The 1973 Supreme Court ruling establishing a constitutional right to abortion under the right to privacy.
A proposed constitutional amendment designed to guarantee equal legal rights for all American citizens regardless of sex.
Conservative activist who led the successful 'STOP ERA' campaign, arguing the amendment threatened traditional family values.

mistakes.w: Saying JFK successfully passed all of his New Frontier laws.
mistakes.r: JFK faced stiff opposition in Congress and failed to pass most of his major social legislation, such as federal aid to education and national health insurance.
Medicare is for the elderly (65+), while Medicaid is for low-income individuals of any age.

mistakes.w: Believing NOW was a radical protest group that burned bras.
mistakes.r: NOW was a mainstream, moderate lobbying and legal organisation modelled on the NAACP; radical feminists used more disruptive direct action.

mistakes.w: Writing that the Equal Rights Amendment successfully became part of the Constitution.
mistakes.r: The ERA failed to gain ratification from the required 38 states by the 1982 deadline and never became law.

mistakes.w: Stating that Roe v. Wade banned abortion nationwide.
mistakes.r: Roe v. Wade legalized abortion nationwide by protecting it under the constitutional right to privacy.

exam.q: What was the purpose of the Peace Corps established by President Kennedy in 1961?
model: To send young American volunteers to developing nations.
To assist with education, health, and agricultural projects to counter Soviet influence.
exam.tip: Keep 2-mark questions brief and factual. Give two clear points or one developed point.

exam.q: Describe two aims of Lyndon B. Johnson's 'Great Society' programme.
model: Aim 1: To end poverty in the United States through federal initiatives like the Economic Opportunity Act.
Aim 2: To end racial injustice and secure civil rights for all Americans, supported by legislation like the Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts.
exam.tip: For a 4-mark 'describe two' question, state two distinct points and add a sentence of expansion/context for each.

exam.q: In what ways were the lives of American women affected by the feminist movement in the 1960s and 1970s?
model: Betty Friedan's book 'The Feminine Mystique' (1963) raised awareness of domestic dissatisfaction and inspired second-wave feminism.
The formation of NOW in 1966 successfully campaigned against sex-segregated job advertisements, enforcing Title VII of the Civil Rights Act.
The Supreme Court case Roe v. Wade (1973) granted women a constitutional right to abortion, increasing reproductive freedom.
However, progress faced strong conservative opposition, notably Phyllis Schlafly's defeat of the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA).
exam.tip: For 8-mark questions, ensure you cover multiple factors (e.g., employment, legal rights, reproductive rights, and opposition) with precise examples.

exam.q: Explain why the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) failed to become law.
model: Organised conservative opposition led by Phyllis Schlafly and her STOP ERA campaign argued it would destroy traditional gender roles.
Critics successfully convinced state legislators that women would lose traditional protections like alimony and exemption from military drafts.
Religious and conservative political groups mobilized against it as part of a broader backlash against 1960s social changes.
It ultimately failed to achieve the necessary ratification from 38 states before the final deadline in 1982.
exam.tip: Focus on cause and consequence. Explain the actions of the opposition and why their arguments resonated with enough state legislators to block ratification.

hist_aqa.3.4.summary: Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal transformed the role of the federal government through the First and Second New Deals, providing relief, recovery, and reform during the Great Depression. While it provided vital aid, reduced unemployment, and created lasting regulatory frameworks, it faced fierce opposition from the Supreme Court, conservatives, and radicals like Huey Long, achieving mixed success for different groups.

core.h: The Context and Aims of the New Deal
core.p: Elected in 1932 by a landslide, Franklin D. Roosevelt promised a **New Deal** for the American people to combat the Great Depression. The policy rested on the Three Rs: Relief for the needy, Economic Recovery, and Reform of financial systems to prevent future crashes.
bullets: Promised decisive government action, contrasting with Hoover's sluggish response.
Relief targeted the immediate needs of the unemployed and starving.
Recovery aimed to revive agriculture and industry through federal intervention.
Reform established long-term safeguards like banking regulations and social security.

callouts.p: FDR's legislative program between 1933 and 1941 designed to relieve poverty, recover the economy, and reform the financial system.
FDR rushed an unprecedented number of reform bills through Congress in his first three months in office.

core.p: The First New Deal focused heavily on immediate relief and economic stabilization. Through radical legislation, the federal government stepped in to rescue the banking system, stabilize agricultural prices, and provide emergency public works jobs.
bullets: Emergency Banking Act: Closed banks for a 'bank holiday' and inspected them before reopening, restoring public trust.
Agricultural Adjustment Act (AAA): Paid farmers subsidies to reduce production and raise crop prices.
National Recovery Administration (NRA): Set codes for fair competition, standard wages, and maximum working hours.
Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC): Provided environmental conservation jobs for young unemployed men.

callouts.p: Always distinguish between First New Deal (relief and recovery) and Second New Deal (reform and long-term security).

core.p: Failing to achieve total economic recovery and facing mounting pressure from radicals, FDR launched the Second New Deal. This phase focused more on social reform, workers' rights, and long-term security for vulnerable Americans.
bullets: Works Progress Administration (WPA): Created millions of jobs not just in construction, but also for artists, writers, and actors.
Social Security Act (1935): Established old-age pensions, unemployment insurance, and federal aid for dependent children.
National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act): Guaranteed workers the right to join unions and engage in collective bargaining.
Resettlement Administration / Farm Security Administration: Aided tenant farmers and sharecroppers.

callouts.p: Often called the Magna Carta of organized labor, it banned unfair employer practices and boosted union membership massively.

core.h: Successes and Limits of the New Deal
core.p: The New Deal had profound successes, but its limits were clear. It saved capitalism, modernized infrastructure, and created a safety net, yet it failed to completely end the Depression—only the massive mobilization of the Second World War finally achieved full employment.
bullets: Success: Restored confidence in banking and government institutions.
Success: Provided relief to millions of destitute citizens and built schools, dams, and hospitals.
Limit: Unemployment remained high until 1941, hovering around 15 percent in 1939.
Limit: Women and ethnic minorities often received lower wages and were excluded from many New Deal benefits.

callouts.p: Do not state that the New Deal ended the Great Depression. The Second World War production boom ended it.

core.h: Impact on Different Groups: African-Americans and Native Americans
core.p: The impact of the New Deal on minority groups was deeply mixed. While some federal programs offered assistance, Southern Democrats ensured that discriminatory local practices were often maintained.
bullets: African-Americans: Benefited from relief programs, but the AAA forced many Black sharecroppers off the land. FDR refused to back an anti-lynching bill for fear of losing Southern white votes.
Black Cabinet: FDR appointed African-American advisors like Mary McLeod Bethune to advise on minority issues.
Indian Reorganization Act (1934): Reversed the Dawes Act, returning land to tribal control and encouraging Native American culture.
Mexican-Americans: Many faced deportation or were excluded from agricultural labor protections under the Wagner Act and Social Security Act.

callouts.p: Key member of FDR's 'Black Cabinet' who advocated for civil rights within New Deal agencies.

core.p: Workers gained unprecedented legal rights through New Deal labor legislation, though women faced institutional discrimination and lower pay in many relief programs.
bullets: Women: Frances Perkins became the first female Cabinet member as Secretary of Labor.
Women: Codes under the NRA routinely permitted lower minimum wages for female workers.
Workers: The Wagner Act and the rise of the CIO led to massive growth in industrial unionism and successful sit-down strikes.
Standard of Living: PWA and WPA projects improved living standards in rural areas through electrification via the Rural Electrification Administration.

callouts.p: A federation of unions that organized workers in industrial mass production on an industry-wide basis.

core.h: Opposition to the New Deal: The Supreme Court
core.p: The conservative Supreme Court posed a major threat to FDR's legislative agenda, striking down key pillars of the First New Deal by ruling that the federal government had overstepped its constitutional powers.
bullets: Schechter Poultry Corporation v. United States (1935): The Court ruled the NRA unconstitutional because it gave legislative powers to the executive branch and regulated intrastate commerce.
United States v. Butler (1936): The Court struck down the AAA, ruling that agricultural regulation was a state matter.
FDR's Court-Packing Scheme (1937): Proposed adding up to six new Supreme Court justices to tilt the balance in his favor.
Outcome: The scheme failed politically and shocked Congress, but the Court began ruling in favor of New Deal legislation anyway ('the switch in time that saved nine').

callouts.p: FDR failed to pass his court-packing bill, but it successfully intimidated the existing justices into halting their anti-New Deal rulings.

core.h: Political Opposition: Radical Critics and the Liberty League
core.p: FDR faced criticism from both the political right, who felt he was becoming a dictator, and the left, who felt he was not doing enough to redistribute wealth.
bullets: American Liberty League: Formed by wealthy conservatives and businessmen who claimed the New Deal destroyed individual liberty and resembled socialism.
Huey Long: Senator from Louisiana who proposed the 'Share Our Wealth' program, taxing millionaires to give every family a home and an income of $5,000.
Father Charles Coughlin: The 'Radio Priest' who initially supported FDR but turned against him, blaming bankers and Jewish people for the Depression.
Dr. Francis Townsend: Proposed a generous pension for the elderly, forcing FDR to implement the Social Security Act to appease his supporters.

callouts.p: Huey Long's radical plan to confiscate large fortunes and guarantee every American family a basic income and home.

core.p: FDR's personal political skill, charisma, and masterful use of the media were central to the survival and implementation of the New Deal.
bullets: Fireside Chats: Radio broadcasts where FDR spoke directly to millions of Americans in a calm, reassuring tone, building immense trust.
Political Pragmatist: FDR was not tied to a single ideology; he experimented with different policies to see what worked.
Master Politician: He skillfully managed Congress, worked with party bosses, and used his landslide mandates to pressure lawmakers.
Empathy and Visibility: Despite being disabled by polio, FDR projected vitality and genuine concern for the 'forgotten man'.

callouts.p: FDR's radio broadcasts that revolutionized political communication and maintained high public morale.

analogy.t: The New Deal is like a massive emergency rescue and home renovation project after a hurricane.
analogy.p: FDR arrives as the new contractor, immediately boarding up broken windows (banking holiday), handing out emergency food and blankets (relief programs), and then rebuilding the foundations with earthquake-proof codes (social security and labor laws). However, some neighbors complain the renovations cost too much and interfere with property rights (Supreme Court and Liberty League), while others argue the new rooms aren't big enough for everyone (minorities and radicals). The analogy breaks down because a house renovation eventually ends, whereas the federal government's permanent expansion altered American governance forever.

terms.d: FDR's program of federal legislation (1933–1941) aimed at relief, recovery, and reform.
The first period of FDR's presidency where a whirlwind of emergency legislation was passed.
Popular names given to the various government agencies created under the New Deal (e.g., AAA, CCC, WPA).
FDR's failed 1937 attempt to increase the number of Supreme Court justices to secure a pro-New Deal majority.
1935 legislation protecting workers' rights to unionize and engage in collective bargaining.
1935 law creating federal old-age pensions, unemployment compensation, and aid to dependents.
Radio broadcasts by FDR to explain his policies directly to the American public.
Democratic Senator and radical critic of FDR who proposed the 'Share Our Wealth' program.
Conservative organization formed in 1934 to oppose the New Deal as dictatorial and socialist.
Secretary of Labor under FDR and the first female cabinet member in US history.

mistakes.w: Saying the New Deal ended the Great Depression.
mistakes.r: State clearly that only the mobilization for the Second World War brought full economic recovery.

mistakes.w: Confusing the First and Second New Deals.
mistakes.r: First New Deal focused on immediate relief and economic stabilization; Second New Deal focused on reform and social security.

mistakes.w: Believing FDR successfully packed the Supreme Court.
mistakes.r: The court-packing bill was defeated in Congress, though the Court changed its rulings anyway.

mistakes.w: Assuming African-Americans universally benefited from the New Deal.
mistakes.r: Many New Deal programs discriminated against Black Americans, notably the AAA and NRA wage codes.

mistakes.w: Thinking the American Liberty League supported FDR's welfare policies.
mistakes.r: They were conservative businessmen who believed the New Deal was creeping socialism.

exam.q: Describe two problems faced by Franklin D. Roosevelt when he became President in 1933.
model: Massive unemployment crippled the economy, with roughly 25 percent of the workforce jobless.
The American banking system had collapsed, causing widespread panic and loss of savings.
exam.tip: Keep descriptions concise; two distinct points are needed for full marks.

exam.q: In what ways were the lives of Americans affected by the Second New Deal?
model: The Social Security Act provided old-age pensions and unemployment insurance, giving financial security to millions.
The Wagner Act legalized collective bargaining, leading to massive growth in trade union membership.
The Works Progress Administration (WPA) created millions of jobs in construction and the arts.
However, minority groups still faced discrimination, and full economic recovery had not yet been achieved.
exam.tip: Ensure you cover multiple areas (e.g. workers, elderly, unemployed) and include a balanced judgment.

exam.q: Which of the following was more important in opposing the New Deal: the Supreme Court or political critics like Huey Long?
model: Explain the Supreme Court's role in striking down key legislation like the AAA and NRA.
Explain the threat posed by Huey Long's 'Share Our Wealth' movement and populist appeal.
Compare their impacts: the Court directly dismantled laws, while critics pressured FDR politically.
Reach a supported judgment on which was more dangerous to FDR's program.
exam.tip: Write a balanced essay with a clear introduction and conclusion evaluating relative significance.

exam.q: Explain why the Supreme Court opposed Roosevelt's New Deal.
model: Conservative justices believed federal alphabet agencies violated the US Constitution.
They ruled that the federal government overstepped its powers by regulating commerce that belonged to individual states (e.g., Schechter Poultry case).
exam.tip: Focus on constitutional and legal arguments used by the justices.

exam.q: Study Source A. How useful is Source A to a historian studying the opposition of the Supreme Court to the New Deal?
model: Analyze the provenance (who wrote it, when, why) for reliability and limitations.
Evaluate the content of the source against own knowledge of the Court-packing crisis or Schechter ruling.
Explain how its tone or perspective limits or enhances its usefulness.
exam.tip: Always judge both provenance (NCP) and content.
